10066-gunman-s-reckoning:
Max Brand's 1921 western opens in Jericho Pass, where fifty empty freight cars dance and roll and rattle on the rough roadbed, filling the pass with thunder. The big engine labors at the grade, but five cars back the locomotive's noise is lost, and a brakie talks above the racket in a nasal overtone.

From that noisy start, Brand builds a gunman's story of reckoning: debts, enemies, and a code that must be paid. His hero moves through cattle country with speed and grit. Readers get a classic Brand western, where a train's thunder gives way to a gunfighter's quiet arithmetic.
10120-england-of-my-heart-spring:
Edward Hutton walked the old pilgrim road through Kent in spring for this 1914 travel book, with pictures by Gordon Home. He follows the route toward Canterbury, pausing at Dartford, Rochester, Faversham, and small towns along the way. The book belongs to a series on England, season by season, and treats place as living history.

Hutton links Roman Kent, the Weald and marsh, Rye and Winchelsea, and the field of Hastings to the lanes he walks. Churches, castles, and country scenes prompt notes on saints, kings, and ordinary folk. Readers get a gentle, learned ramble through English spring, rich in local lore and place names.
1016-on-the-improvement-of-the-understan:
Baruch Spinoza wrote this treatise on the improvement of the understanding, also called the Treatise on the Emendation of the Intellect, translated by R. H. M. Elwes. Its contents run from the ordinary objects of men's desires to the true and final good, with certain rules of life and four modes of perception.

Spinoza asks how the mind can rise from confused ideas to true knowledge, and how that knowledge can guide a good life. His prose is clear and searching, though the work breaks off unfinished. The treatise is a fine introduction to Spinoza, and a classic essay on how to think well.
1022-walking:
Henry David Thoreau praises the act of walking out into wild land as a spiritual and political need, not a mere pastime. In this essay, drawn from his lectures, he urges readers to leave town, road, and clock behind and let swamp, wood, and field reset the mind.

Thoreau claims that wildness keeps the world sane, and that a man who walks well thinks well. His sentences stride and halt like a walker, full of jokes, lists, and sudden aphorisms. The piece helped seed the love of wild places in America, and it still calls readers outdoors.
10220-daddy-takes-us-skating:
Howard R. Garis wrote this children's book in 1914, for the young readers of his Daddy series. Brother and sister Hal and Mab Blake ask their father about everything, from red noses in cold weather to steam engines. Daddy answers with patience, turning each question into a small lesson.

When winter comes, Daddy takes the children skating, and the ice brings falls, fun, and fresh questions about frost, skates, and safety. Friends join the outings, and home talk rounds out each day. Readers get a gentle, chatty picture of family life, curiosity, and winter play.
10274-sermons-on-evil-speaking:
Isaac Barrow, a seventeenth-century Cambridge scholar and divine, preached these sermons on the sins of speech. A later editor, Henry Morley, framed them with a life of Barrow, who rose from Charterhouse and Trinity College to wide fame as a preacher. The sermons treat talk not as trifle, but as a moral act with real harm.

Barrow attacks foolish jesting, rash swearing, slander, and gossip in general, showing how each wounds hearers and speakers alike. His arguments are close, learned, and often sharp, rooted in Scripture and reason. Readers get a stern, thoughtful guide to guarding the tongue, still clear on why careless words matter.
10323-the-rover-boys-at-college-or-the-r:
Arthur M. Winfield, a pen name used for the Rover Boys series, published this college tale in 1910. Dick, Tom, and Sam Rover leave school days behind for college, where new friends, sports, and rivals await. The subtitle warns that two roads lie open: the right one and the wrong one.

Hazing, a colors contest, rowing, football, a haunted house, and a charge of disgrace test the brothers in turn. Girls arrive, misunderstandings grow, and evidence at last sorts friends from foes. Readers get a lively, moral boys' story of college fun, fair play, and growing up.
10395-joy-and-power-three-messages-with-:
Henry van Dyke gathered three messages in this 1903 book, delivered at Los Angeles, Princeton, and Harvard within weeks of each other. Van Dyke, a preacher and writer, says the three talks, though shaped for different hearers, point one way and urge one course. Their shared meaning is the best he had learned in life.

Joy and Power treats religion and happiness, The Battle of Life treats struggle and duty, and The Good Old Way treats faith's steady path. Each message joins joy to action, not to mere feeling. Readers get warm, eloquent sermons on living well, useful for students of American preaching.
1046-god-the-invisible-king:
H. G. Wells sets out his own faith in this 1917 book: not the creeds of the churches, but belief in a personal God who strives with men against evil. He rejects an all-powerful, all-knowing deity and pictures instead a finite, striving king who needs human help to win. The book speaks in plain, urgent prose.

Wells sketches a modern religion of conduct, with chapters on sin, prayer, and what a church could be. He wrote amid the slaughter of war, seeking a faith that could face it. The book stirred both praise and scorn, and it gives a frank window on one famous mind wrestling with God.
1049-vanished-arizona-recollections-of-t:
Martha Summerhayes, a young bride from New England, followed her army officer husband to the Arizona frontier in the 1870s and wrote down what she found. Her memoir moves from sea voyages and desert marches to lonely forts, where officers' wives kept house with few goods and much grit.

She writes of Apache scouts, rough roads, childbirth far from help, and the odd kindness of army life. Her eye is sharp and her tone frank, with humor about her own greenhorn days. The book gives a rare woman's view of the frontier army, and it reads as both history and a good yarn.
10630-coming-to-the-king:
Frances Ridley Havergal, a well-known English writer of hymns and devotional verse, wrote Coming to the King as a poem of prayer. The poem takes a text from Solomon's story in the first book of Kings. Its speaker comes alone to the King of Salem, as the Queen of Sheba once came, but with no train and no costly gifts. Only requests and questions are brought to the throne.

The poem follows that meeting: the speaker tells the King all that weighs on the heart and hears answers that bring guidance, victory over doubt, and quiet rest. Short lines and simple images carry the whole piece. Readers looking for gentle, earnest Christian verse will find here a clear example of Havergal's devotional voice.
1075-the-strength-of-the-strong:
Jack London gathers tales of men who live by muscle and nerve: hunters, fighters, and outcasts who test each other in a world where law is thin. The title story pits tribe against tribe in a fable of how the strong rule, and how the weak learn to band together. Other tales range from the sea to the prize ring.

London writes with his usual force, praising grit while showing its cost in blood and pride. His people are blunt, his scenes are stark, and his endings seldom spare anyone. The book gives a compact dose of London's creed, and it suits readers who like short tales with a punch.
1076-the-wallet-of-kai-lung:
Ernest Bramah's Kai Lung, a wandering Chinese storyteller, opens his wallet of tales for Western readers: fables of mandarins, merchants, and rogues, each told in grave, ornate English that mimics Chinese courtesy. The stories turn on wit, fate, and the traps set by greed.

Kai Lung himself frames the tales, dodging robbers and officials with a story at the right hour. Bramah, an Englishman who never visited China, built a whole imagined East from books and fancy. The book charmed a generation, and it gave fantasy its first great Chinese voice, however fanciful.
10794-dahcotah-life-and-legends-of-the-s:
Mary Eastman wrote Dahcotah, or Life and Legends of the Sioux Around Fort Snelling, from her residence at the Minnesota fort, with a preface by Mrs. C. M. Kirkland and drawings by Captain Eastman. Dedicated to Henry Sibley of the House of Representatives, the book records Sioux daily life, customs, and stories as Eastman saw and heard them.

Eastman writes with sympathy, hoping purity of heart and learning will serve the good of others, including Native peoples. Her legends preserve tales told near the fort in the mid-nineteenth century. Readers get an early, firsthand account of Dakota life, valuable despite the limits of its time.
10818-sport-and-work-on-the-nepaul-front:
Writing as "Maori," an indigo planter published Sport and Work on the Nepaul Frontier in 1878, after twelve years in India and a visit home in 1875. A frontispiece of tiger hunting on the return to camp sets the tone. The author found visitors at home ignorant of ordinary Indian life, and wrote a chatty, unpretentious book for friends about daily toil and play.

Chapters cover planting work, sport, servants, neighbors, and the frontier country itself. The tone is familiar rather than grand, full of anecdote. Readers get a planter's-eye view of British India in the 1860s and 1870s, lively and personal.
10850-philaster-or-love-lies-a-bleeding:
Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher's Philaster, or Love Lies a Bleeding, is a Jacobean tragicomedy set in Sicily. Its persons include the King, Philaster the heir to the crown, Pharamond prince of Spain, Arethusa the king's daughter, and Eufrasia, daughter of Dion, disguised as the page Bellario. Lords, ladies, citizens, and woodmen fill the scene.

The plot turns on love, jealousy, and mistaken identity, as Philaster loves Arethusa while Bellario's secret devotion complicates all. The play ends in the mingled tears and reconciliations of tragicomedy. Readers meet Beaumont and Fletcher at their romantic best, in verse of grace and passion.
10916-parent-and-child-volume-iii-child-:
Mosiah Hall wrote Parent and Child, volume three, Child Study and Training, in 1916 for the Deseret Sunday School Union of Salt Lake City. Its introduction calls home-making and child-rearing the fundamental business of the world, needing knowledge as well as love. Loving hearts suffer, Hall warns, from mistakes that loving intelligence might have prevented.

The volume urges parents to study child nature and the laws of development, so they can guide children wisely. Its tone is earnest, practical, and rooted in Sunday school teaching. Parents and teachers get an early twentieth-century guide to raising children with understanding.
1118-much-ado-about-nothing:
In Messina, the witty Beatrice and Benedick trade insults while their friends trick them into love, and the young Claudio, fooled by a villain's plot, shames his bride Hero at the altar. William Shakespeare's comedy balances sparkling wordplay with a near-tragedy of honor and slander.

Hero's seeming death and the unmasking of Don John set all right, and the two pairs marry amid jokes and dances. Dogberry, the bumbling constable, steals scenes with his mangled speech. The play's mix of laughter and hurt keeps it among Shakespeare's most loved comedies.
1328-the-tinker-s-wedding:
J. M. Synge's short comedy follows Michael Byrne, a tinker who wants to marry his sweetheart Sarah Casey. The priest who would wed them demands a price, and the tinkers' tricks undo the bargain. The play moves through a country roadside with wit and a touch of blasphemy.

Synge writes the tinkers' speech with music and mischief, and the play's joke cuts both ways: priest and tinkers each want their due. The comedy, once banned from the Abbey stage, now stands as a small gem of Irish theatre, funny and sharp.
1457-mistress-wilding:
Rafael Sabatini's romance of the Monmouth Rebellion follows Ruth Westmacott, called Mistress Wilding, and the men who love and imperil her in the west of England. Sir Rowland comes to her rescue, Diana schemes against her, and a forced marriage, a duel, and a counterstroke drive the plot through the troubled summer of 1685.

Sabatini writes with dash and colour, filling the tale with cavaliers, rebels, and narrow escapes. The heroine's spirit holds the centre. It is a brisk historical romance in the Sabatini manner, full of swordplay, intrigue, and honour tested under a failing cause.
1487-the-perfect-wagnerite-a-commentary-:
Bernard Shaw's commentary reads Wagner's Ring cycle as a drama of ideas rather than a fairy tale of gods and gold. Wotan, Brunnhilde, and Siegfried become figures of power, law, love, and revolution, and Shaw argues that the cycle's true subject is the modern world and its coming change.

Shaw writes with wit and force, praising Wagner's music drama while quarrelling with its philosophy, especially in the final opera. The book, first written for German readers, helped English audiences take Wagner seriously as a thinker. It remains a bracing, partisan guide to the Ring.
1519-much-ado-about-nothing:
Shakespeare's Messina comedy, in this improved text, again pairs Claudio and Hero, whose wedding Don John wrecks with a lie about Hero's honour. Beatrice and Benedick, enemies in wit whom friends trick into confessing love. A night watch of blundering constables overhears the plot and saves Hero's name.

Masked dances, garden eavesdropping, and a wedding turned to accusation give the play its sparkle and its sting. Beatrice's demand that Benedick kill Claudio marks its serious heart. Much Ado is Shakespeare's most balanced comedy, where laughter and honour sit side by side.
1520-much-ado-about-nothing:
Set in Messina after a war, Much Ado follows two pairs of lovers: Claudio and Hero, whose wedding is wrecked by a villain's lie. Beatrice and Benedick, witty enemies tricked into love by their friends. Don John, the bastard prince, plots against Hero's honour, and only a watchman's blundering arrests save the day.

Through masked balls, eavesdropping, and a wedding that ends in accusation, Shakespeare mixes farce with near-tragedy. Beatrice and Benedick's merry war remains the play's delight. It is a sparkling comedy about gossip, honour, and how easily a good name can be lost and won back.
1561-pagan-and-christian-creeds-their-or:
Edward Carpenter's Pagan and Christian Creeds argues that the world's religions are lame attempts to represent one root fact: the central universal life. Creeds, rituals, and ceremonies, he holds, symbolise in rude form the redemption and fulfilment of our most intimate natures, whether pagan or Christian.

Carpenter traces shared myths of dying gods, saviours, and sacred seasons, and asks what Christianity owes to older faiths. His tone is earnest and speculative. The book is a classic of early comparative religion, dated in method but still stimulating for readers interested in myth and faith.
1613-count-bunker-being-a-bald-yet-verac:
J. Storer Clouston's Count Bunker continues the adventures of two gentlemen first met in The Lunatic at Large, now chronicled baldly yet veraciously. A supposed count arrives in English society, where polite interest masks sharp curiosity, and imposture, romance, and a run of comic scrapes follow.

Clouston writes with dry, Edwardian wit, letting his rogues talk their way into and out of trouble. The chronicle is light and episodic. Count Bunker is a pleasant sequel for readers who enjoy tales of plausible scoundrels loose among the respectable. Readers who enjoy rogue tales will find it light fun.
1675-new-forces-in-old-china-an-inevitab:
Arthur Judson Brown writes on new forces in old China, arguing that an inevitable awakening was under way as reform, missions, trade, and education pressed on the empire. Brown, a missionary secretary, knew China at first hand. Brown, secretary of the Presbyterian Board of Foreign Missions, visited China often.

He describes railways, schools, and new ideas alongside old customs, and he predicts change that few in the West then foresaw. The book captures Western hopes and fears about China at the turn of the century. His awakening theme looked to schools, railways, and a new press to change old China.
1753-swan-song:
An old actor named Svetlovidov is left alone in an empty theatre after the audience has gone. He talks to the prompter about the roles he will never play again. Left alone after the audience has gone, Svetlovidov talks to the prompter, remembers his roles, and faces the fact that his art and his life are both nearly over.

The piece runs barely half an hour in performance. It holds Chekhov's whole view of the theatre: glory remembered, youth gone, and a man who can still move an audience of one. It is often paired with The Sea-Gull in collections. It shows the younger Chekhov already writing about age and loss with the restraint that marks his later plays.
1959-the-crown-of-thorns-a-token-for-the:
E. H. Chapin's Crown of Thorns, a token for the sorrowing, gathers discourses written for the bereaved. A preface explains that one sermon, The Mission of Little Children, was written just after the death of a dear son and first published as a pamphlet. The edition having become exhausted, Chapin reprints it here.

The sermons ask what mortal existence is, into which we crowd so much interest and over whose uncertain future we project our plans so confidently. They answer with Christian comfort. The book is a work of pastoral care rather than of argument, and its value lies in its tone: a minister speaking to grief without preaching at it.
1966-the-path-of-the-king:
John Buchan's Path of the King, dedicated to his wife and first read by a Cotswold fire. It traces a single idea through history: that a kingly spirit passes from age to age, carried by ordinary people. The chapters run from Hightown under Sunfell through the Englishman, the Wife of Flanders, and the Maid, to Eaucourt by the waters and beyond.

Travellers meet athwart their road and exchange greetings. On the second morning they reach a city populous in men but not in houses, with lines of skin tents stretching for miles. Buchan writes history as romance, and the book's charm lies in its chain of linked lives, each one carrying the same light a little further.
19869-while-caroline-was-growing:
Josephine Daskam Bacon wrote While Caroline Was Growing in 1906. Caroline is a girl whose heart outruns her lessons. She chants her geography by rote: bounded in the north by Massachusetts. Her eyes are not on the map at all. Like the gentleman in the poem, her thoughts are far away. Bacon watches girlhood with that divided attention in mind.

Bacon's stories of girls were praised for their truth. Caroline daydreams, schemes, and grows by small increments. Nothing in the book condescends to its young heroine. The New England setting stays light in the background. Readers meet a real child, not a lesson in skirts. The book charms by observation rather than event.
19875-the-bobbin-boy-or-how-nat-got-his-:
The Bobbin Boy tells how Nat got his learning, as an example for youth. Its opening is a bright May morning scene. A fenced patch of ground, a few trees, and birdsong frame it. Nat stands with his hoe in hand. His father gives directions for the work. The boy who hoes here will work in a textile mill. Nathaniel Peabody Banks is the bobbin boy of the title.

Banks rose from mill boy to Civil War general and congressman. William Makepeace Thayer wrote his life for boys to copy. Bobbin boys tended spinning frames for tiny wages. Thayer turns that start into a ladder of self-help. The book is pure nineteenth-century success gospel. It shows the genre's faith in industry and schooling.
19924-plain-facts-for-old-and-young:
John Harvey Kellogg wrote Plain Facts for Old and Young, a famous Victorian health guide. It treats sex, reproduction, and personal habits with unusual frankness. Kellogg prefaced the practical part with reproductive anatomy. He took special pains, he says, to avoid anything like indelicacy. The description stays concise and clinical by his era's lights. The book sold enormously for decades.

Kellogg ran the Battle Creek Sanitarium and preached total health reform. Plain Facts mixes sound advice with stern moral warnings. Its chapters on chastity and habit alarmed and fascinated readers. Historians of medicine and sexuality cite it constantly. It shows Victorian purity culture in its own words. Few health books reveal their age so completely.
19931-the-reckoning:
Percival Wilde wrote The Reckoning as a one-act play. A barber mixes his lather while trading life stories. His customer has moved around so much, he says, that he is neither Southerner nor Northerner. He lived a year in a little town near Savannah. The chair, the lather, and the talk set a trap of coziness. Wilde's one-acts usually spring such traps late. The reckoning of the title waits offstage.

Wilde specialized in short plays with a final twist. Barbershop talk lets strangers confess more than they mean. A razor in hand raises the stakes quietly. The Southern year will surely matter before the curtain. This piece shows Wilde's economy and menace. It is a small masterclass in one-act construction.
20069-caruso-and-tetrazzini-on-the-art-o:
Enrico Caruso and Luisa Tetrazzini were two of the great opera voices of their age. In Caruso and Tetrazzini on the Art of Singing, both share how they trained and sang. Tetrazzini sang Inez in Meyerbeer's L'Africaine before an Italian crowd. Queen Margherita heard her, praised her, and foresaw a great career.

The book mixes life tales with plain advice on voice and craft. A young singer then earned a hundred dollars a month, a rare start. Readers who sing, or love opera, get tips from stars. Their fame gives weight to each small point on breath and tone.
20146-engineering-bulletin-no-1-boiler-a:
Rufus T. Strohm wrote Engineering Bulletin No. 1, on boiler and furnace testing. The United States Fuel Administration backed daily checks of boiler plants. The simplest test, the bulletin says, is an evaporation test. It shows how well a boiler and furnace truly work each day.

Fuel was precious in wartime, and waste cost money and coal alike. Plant men could use these steps with tools they had at hand. The bulletin lays out method, care, and records in plain order. It stands as a neat piece of practical engineering from the fuel-saving era.
20187-on-christmas-day-in-the-morning:
On Christmas Day in the Morning is a Christmas tale of home and longing. Gay Nan reads a letter and feels a choke rise in her throat. She tells her husband Sam they must be there next Christmas. Sam agrees at once, with cheer and warmth in his voice.

Sam only wishes he still had a father and mother to visit. That wish gives the tale its ache beneath the holiday glow. Family homes draw grown children back each year at Christmas time. Readers get a short, tender tale of letters, loss, and promised returns.
20349-the-moving-picture-girls-at-rocky-:
Laura Lee Hope published The Moving Picture Girls at Rocky Ranch in 1914. Ruth De Vere is told that film work teaches words that mean something. Sign-post words, by contrast, merely point and carry no life in them. Her sister is glad to see her getting sensible at last.

Are you ready to go to the studio, she asks Ruth. At Rocky Ranch, the girls film western scenes among real cowboys. Great days among the cowboys, the subtitle promises its young readers. The book mixes film craft, ranch life, and sisterly banter throughout.
20367-the-coming-of-the-king:
Set in the ancient land of Judea under Roman rule, The Coming of the King tells a story from the time of Christ. A craftsman fashions a heavy yoke while word spreads of a grim order. Timber is being cut near Mount Tabor for two thousand crosses, and fear hangs over the workers.

The tale builds its drama from the lives of ordinary people living under that threat. Talk of mercy, dread, and a coming king runs through the scenes. Readers who enjoy Bible-era fiction will find a vivid picture of village life in a land waiting for change.
20386-embroidery-and-tapestry-weaving:
Mrs. Archibald H. Christie wrote Embroidery and Tapestry Weaving as a guide to the history and craft of needlework. The book covers both design and workmanship. It treats stitching and loom work as serious arts with long pasts.

Christie points readers to fine surviving pieces, including fragments worked in the tenth century. She singles out the great period of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, with many examples kept at the South Kensington Museum. Workers get practical help, while students of art get a clear survey of how the craft grew.
20519-highways-in-hiding:
Highways in Hiding, published in 1956, is a science fiction novel by George O. Smith. Its narrator, Steve Cornell, belongs to a world where some people hide powers of the mind. An underground network, the Highways, shields them from a hostile public.

Cornell knows what happens to the exposed. The Highways crowd, he says, had enough savvy to clean up any mess before their bodies got cold. Without that protection, men like him would not last. Smith mixes road adventure with telepathy and pursuit, in a tale from the golden age of magazine science fiction.
20526-short-story-writing:
Charles Raymond Barrett's Short Story Writing is a practical textbook for people learning to write fiction. Barrett breaks the short story into its working parts. Every element, he insists, must lead up to something in the finished tale.

A story needs for its structure a plot, a bit of life, an incident. Such an incident might come from a brief newspaper paragraph. Barrett shows how Richard Harding Davis could take the substance of just such a paragraph and build a story on it. The book served the many Americans who hoped to sell stories to the booming magazines.
20656-old-christmas-from-the-sketch-book:
Washington Irving's Old Christmas, drawn from his Sketch Book, describes Christmas at an English country hall. Irving visited England and fell in love with its old customs. The piece follows the squire's Christmas from the guests' arrival to the great dinner.

An old song in the text praises the season. A man might then behold, at Christmas, in each hall, good fires to curb the cold and meat for great and small. The neighbors were friendly bidden, and all had welcome true. The poor from the gates were not turned away. Irving's sketch shaped how America imagined the old English Christmas.
20728-space-viking:
Lucas Trask dreams of showing his bride the new house on Traskon, then taking a long trip among the Sword Worlds. H. Beam Piper sets that tender plan against worlds with names like Excalibur, Morglay, and Flamberge. War has already flared again on Durendal, so peace feels thin from the first pages.

Space Viking follows a wronged man who turns raider among rough star worlds. Piper mixes revenge, trade, statecraft, and battle in a tight plot. The book is famed for treating space piracy as real politics, not mere noise. It is a key work in Piper's future history.
20770-apple-growing:
Apples can be used in more ways than most fruits, says M. C. Burritt in Apple-Growing. Better knowledge of the fruit's worth has raised its use, he notes. New ways to prepare it for the table helped that growth along.

Orchard work fills the guide, from choosing ground to picking and selling fruit. Burritt wrote for growers who needed sound, plain advice in one book. Varieties, pests, pruning, and packing all get their share. The book shows a time when apples were big business for small farms. Its care with detail still speaks to anyone who tends fruit trees today.
20813-how-lisa-loved-the-king:
Palermo holds high festival in How Lisa Loved the King, a poem by George Eliot. Matrons and maidens watch a mock tournament where safe sport hints at danger. The scene takes a lift, as from epic song, the verse itself declares.

Eliot, famed for great novels, also wrote verse tales of real craft. Lisa's love for a king far above her rank drives this one. Sicily's sun, court pomp, and a maid's bold heart fill the lines. The poem shows the young Eliot testing themes of rank, longing, and women's inner lives that her novels later made immortal.
20836-ting-a-ling:
Aufalia takes a spring walk, veiled, with two grim slaves at her heels. Frank R. Stockton opens Ting-a-Ling, from 1882, in a town of secluded suburbs. Birds sing, crocuses bloom, and a fairy tale mood settles at once.

Stockton, famed for The Lady or the Tiger, wrote droll fairy tales with a twist. Ting-a-Ling, a tiny being, lends the book its name and spark. Magic, wit, and odd turns fill these tales for young and old alike. Stockton's dry humor sets his fairy work apart from sweeter fare, and this book shows it in full, playful flight.
20896-carry-s-rose-or-the-magic-of-kindn:
Caroline coaxes her lamb Daisy to wait, for wheels sound at the avenue gate. Mrs. George Cupples opens Carry's Rose, a tale for the young, with that bright arrival. Clapping hands and keen hopes set the tale's warm tone at once.

Kindness works like magic in Cupples's story of a girl and her rose. Small gifts, patience, and love turn hearts across the plot. Cupples wrote tales for children with a gentle, Scottish warmth. This one keeps her mark: home scenes, beast friends, and a clear moral that never needs to raise its voice to be heard.
21024-the-angels-song:
Bonfires blaze on hilltops and steeples ring as a king's heir enters life, The Angel's Song marvels. Nations feast while prayers rise to Him by whom kings reign, it says. All that pomp frames its turn to a far humbler birth.

Thomas Binney's famed sermon sets Christ's birth against the pomp of earthly thrones. No bells or feasts marked the manger, yet angels sang above it. Binney, a great Nonconformist preacher, builds that contrast with fire. The sermon became a Christmas classic in chapels, prized for its sweep from palace noise to the still, high song over Bethlehem.
21032-exercises-in-knitting:
Stitch counts head each pattern in Exercises in Knitting, so any piece can be resized at will. Open patterns suit Shetland shawls, Cornelia Mee notes, while chair covers run in coloured wools. White work, she adds, wants linen thread number one.

Mee's patterns teach doilies, covers, shawls, and trims stitch by patient stitch. Victorian knitters kept such books by the work basket for daily use. Colours and shades are named so each piece can be matched at home. The book keeps a whole craft dialect alive: counts, threads, and the small maths of the needle, set down with care.
21134-working-in-the-shade-lowly-sowing-:
Curiosity runs high in the small town of Franchope when Riverton Park, empty for twenty years, is to be occupied again. The Reverend Theodore P. Wilson builds his tale around the new arrival at Park House. The house is a fine old mansion on rising ground in a rich park. Episodes of selfishness and unselfishness drive the plot.

Wilson treats his theme almost as a sermon in story form: selfish acts lead toward disaster, while quiet, unselfish sowing leads upward. He had won a literary prize for Frank Oldfield some ten years earlier with the same method. The book stays short, direct, and intent on leaving readers with food for thought.
21372-steve-young:
Steve Young, sixteen and an orphan, joins a rescue voyage to the icy seas in George Manville Fenn's tale. His uncle, Captain Young, has vanished on a voyage toward Spitzbergen, and the captain's friends charter a Norwegian vessel, the Hvalross, to search for him. The ship's doctor thinks boys are a nuisance and says so.

Polar bears, killing cold, gales, ice floes, and the total dark of the arctic winter test the party. A cowardly young Highlander provides the comedy. At last they find Captain Young and most of his crew alive. Fenn fills the search with the practical detail of ice navigation he loved to teach.
21400-style-in-singing:
W. E. Haslam sets out what makes singing artful in Style in Singing, published by G. Schirmer in 1911. Haslam wrote the book for his own pupils, and he says the field lacked such a guide. Books on how to play instruments with style were common, but not books on song.

He ranks the parts of a singer's craft in clear order. Pose and technique must be sound before style can be learned, he argues. Yet skill alone is not enough without style to crown it. A well-chosen stock of songs, fitted to each voice, completes the training he lays out.
21534-textiles-and-clothing:
Kate Heintz Watson wrote Textiles and Clothing for the American School of Home Economics in 1907. Watson taught domestic art at the Lewis Institute and lectured at the University of Chicago. The book forms one part of a twelve-volume home-study course on homemaking.

The course claimed near three thousand pages and a thousand pictures across its set. Watson treats fibres, weaves, and the care and choice of cloth for dress and home. Experts in home economics across several colleges backed the series. Mothers, teachers, nurses, and house managers formed its target readers, in an age when home study promised a new profession for women.
21636-bluff-crag-or-a-good-word-costs-no:
Mrs George Cupples writes for the young in Bluff Crag, or A Good Word Costs Nothing, issued in 1872. Cupples also wrote The Story of Our Doll and The Little Captain. Nelson of London, Edinburgh, and New York published the tale.

Mr Lincoln hides behind his newspaper while children wait by the fire for his thoughts. His breathing soon shows he has fallen asleep instead of thinking. Small scenes of home life carry the book's lesson, set in the title. A good word costs nothing, and the tale shows its worth at Bluff Crag and beyond, in a gentle Victorian key.
21722-a-practical-discourse-on-some-prin:
Poet Robert Bridges turns critic in this short study of how hymns should be sung, first printed in a journal of theology in 1899. The booklet came out at Oxford in 1901, priced at one shilling. Bridges starts from Saint Augustine, who wept at the hymns sung in Milan in the year 386. That plain early music had few tools, yet it stirred Augustine deeply.

From that case, Bridges asks what makes church singing move a hearer: the tune, the words, or the singer's own feeling. He argues for care in how hymns are chosen, set, and sung in church. It is a brief, sharp piece by a poet who cared deeply about both music and verse.
21990-the-campaign-of-1776-around-new-yo:
New York's Revolutionary ordeal is mapped and documented in Henry P. Johnston's The Campaign of 1776 Around New York and Brooklyn, published by the Long Island Historical Society in 1878. Johnston calls the ground pre-eminently Revolutionary soil, where the war came to America's doors. His book gives a fresh, full account of the Battle of Long Island. It covers the loss of New York and reviews events to the year's close.

Maps compiled by the author, portraits, and original documents fill out the narrative. Spelling in quoted papers stands as written, down to the doubled letters marked with macrons. Johnston wrote as Brooklyn's own historian of its founding battle. The work remains a standard, source-rich history of the campaign that nearly ended the Revolution.
22029-spool-knitting:
Mary A. McCormack's Spool Knitting, published in 1909, teaches children to knit with a simple spool and pegs. McCormack compares the child at work to a spider moving round its web. The toy knitter makes cord in a round web, a flat web, or a circular mat. From those basics the lessons build quickly.

Projects include a ball and rattle for a baby, caps, mittens, slippers, and bootees. Dolls get muffs, hoods, coats, and collarettes of their own. Each piece needs only cord, patience, and a small pair of hands. The book is a neat window on the craft teaching once given to young girls.
22098-the-seventh-day-sabbath-a-perpetua:
Joseph Bates, a retired sea captain turned Adventist preacher, argued the case for Saturday worship in The Seventh Day Sabbath, a Perpetual Sign. Bates held that the Sabbath runs from creation to the end of time. His tract works through the Bible in order, text by text. When a questioner asks the way to eternal life, Bates notes that Christ points to the commandments.

He answers the common claim that the Sabbath was dropped or moved to Sunday. Scripture, he insists, nowhere leaves the seventh day out. Bates's little book helped found the Sabbatarian Adventist movement. It still states, in plain King James language, the core argument for keeping Saturday holy.
22325-the-art-of-modern-lace-making:
The Art of Modern Lace-Making teaches a craft with very old roots. Its opening claims lace, in one form or another, reaches back to the earliest ages. Even Scripture, it notes, mentions web-like fabrics of rude make.

Those early fabrics share their main traits with modern lace. Skill over centuries turned simple webs into fine, prized work. A practical manual like this one passed that skill to new hands. It treats lace as both art and trade. Readers interested in needlework get period instruction and pride in craft. The book also preserves how makers once explained their art to learners at home.
22379-masters-of-water-colour-painting:
Masters of Water-Colour Painting surveys British artists who worked in watercolor. Its plate list reads like a roll of honored names. Samuel Prout, Paul Sandby, and Thomas Rowlandson all appear.

Sandby's Windsor Castle shows the Round and Devil's Towers. Rowlandson gives the entrance to Vauxhall Gardens in London. James Holland paints a shrine in Venice for one plate. Samuel Prout sets a Venetian palace on the Grand Canal. William Henry Hunt contributes a homely scene, Plucking the Fowl. Francis Towne paints on the River Dart. The book lets readers compare these masters side by side, plate by plate.
22392-essentials-in-conducting:
Essentials in Conducting, issued by the Oliver Ditson Company, teaches leaders of bands and choirs. It defines the conductor's work at the start. He stands before performers and gives his whole effort to directing them.

A conductor of orchestra or chorus does not play or sing himself. His entire time goes to shaping the group's performance. The goal is a musically effective ensemble result. Clear beats, cues, and control make many players act as one. Manuals like this trained school and church musicians across America. Readers get the basics of a craft usually learned by watching. It preserves period teaching on tempo, gesture, and rehearsal discipline.
2240-much-ado-about-nothing:
In Messina, returning soldiers bring love and trouble in equal measure. Much Ado About Nothing pairs the sparring Beatrice and Benedick, tricked into love by their friends, with the young Hero and Claudio, whose wedding collapses on a villain's lie. Shakespeare weaves witty war between the sexes around a darker plot of slander.

Dogberry and his watch bumble toward the truth just in time, and the play ends with dances, forgiveness, and second chances. Its language sparkles, and Beatrice remains one of Shakespeare's liveliest heroines. The comedy still delights audiences who enjoy sharp talk and happy endings earned the hard way.
22482-men-in-the-making:
Ambrose Shepherd wrote Men in the Making, a book on forming character. One early passage follows a thinker who doubted the moon's worship. He did not fall in readily with that worship as he matured.

He became, Shepherd says, one of an order of doubters. The world owes much, he argues, to doubters of that kind. This youth suspected the moon was not a cause in itself. Priests taught otherwise, but he saw an effect needing a cause. Such stories model the growth Shepherd wants in his readers. Men are made, his title insists, by thought, faith, and questioning. The book offers period guidance toward sturdy, reflective manhood.
22554-as-it-was-in-the-beginning:
As It Was in the Beginning, dated 1912, is a novel issued under Desmond Fitzgerald's imprint. Grenville, its cool-headed hero, faces his friend's searching gaze. A glow of exceptional brilliance shines in Grenville's eyes then.

Grenville was not the type to be readily excited, the narrator notes. Yet that glow betrayed feeling as the two men met. He wondered if Fenton could be jesting with him at that moment. Such a charged meeting opens a story of strong emotions held in check. The title hints that first states of things govern later events. Readers get Edwardian fiction of friendship, love, and revelation. Its reserve makes its bursts of feeling count for more.
22574-the-best-portraits-in-engraving:
The Best Portraits in Engraving celebrates the art of the engraved portrait. Its author examined other collections in America before writing. In Paris, the great national cabinet of engravings became his daily medicine.

He underwent severe medical treatment during that Paris stay abroad. For weeks, the vast cabinet counted its holdings by the million. There was everything there to please or instruct a lover of prints. Thinking of those kindly portfolios, he records his gratitude now. They were benefactors to him in a hard season of illness. The book guides readers among master engravers and their sitters. It preserves connoisseurship of a kind photography was already displacing.
22603-rational-horse-shoeing:
Rational Horse-Shoeing, signed Wildair, is a practical manual on shoeing horses without harming their feet. The catalog record gives no year. The author blames many foot diseases on unnatural shoeing and promotes the Goodenough shoe as the sound alternative.

The system, readers are told, is meant for sound horses: to protect the feet and keep them healthy, not to cure disease. Rules in the author's circular cover ordinary cases, with disease treated as the exception needing special care. In an age when horses powered farms and cities, such advice carried real money value. The book now offers farriers and horse historians a clear statement of one reform school of shoeing.
22744-the-adventurous-seven-their-hazard:
Bessie Marchant wrote The Adventurous Seven: Their Hazardous Undertaking, a story of young people facing danger far from home. The catalog record gives no year. Marchant, who published as Bessie Comfort, wrote hundreds of adventure tales, many with brave heroines in wild places, at a time when such books were thought a boys' province.

The sample opens in a village schoolroom packed as full as it would hold, its air so thick that, as Sylvia said, a spoon could nearly scoop it. A stout lecturer perspires freely but means to do his duty, declaiming with tremendous vigor. From that stifling room the seven's undertaking launches. Marchant's pace is rapid and her young people resourceful, making her a pioneer of girls' adventure fiction.
23101-three-thousand-years-of-mental-hea:
George Barton Cutten traces mind cure through the ages in Three Thousand Years of Mental Healing, published in 1911. His epigraph, borrowed from Stowe, celebrates the mind's royal power over flesh. For a season, it claims, belief can armor nerve and muscle like steel, and make weak people strong.

Cutten, a psychologist, surveys the whole road from temple sleep and relics to Christian Science and the Emmanuel movement. He writes as a scholar of a craze, sorting faith, suggestion, and fraud with a cool hand. The book appeared when mental healing filled magazines and split churches. Cutten believed mental influence was genuine. He trusted its salesmen far less, and that double view makes his map of the movement unusually clear.
2315-the-flag-raising:
Kate Douglas Wiggin, author of Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, offers a patriotic story for children centered on a school flag raising. The Flag-Raising follows pupils and teachers as they prepare a ceremony honoring the flag, learning what it stands for along the way. Wiggin's warmth and her belief in children's civic feeling shape every page.

The book is short, earnest, and of its time, with songs and speeches woven into the school day. Modern readers will note its period patriotism. As a piece of children's literature history, it charms.
23185-the-glory-of-ippling:
The Glory of Ippling is a work of science fiction about contact between cultures. Its premise rests on a bold claim: no machine can match a group of humans for sheer complexity, even when those humans are drilled to work with machine-like precision. That idea frames everything the Ipplingers do.

One case follows an Ipplinger Cultural Contact Group handed a well-connected visitor, a Boswellister with important ties. Their orders are to place him on an assignment meant to test his maturity. Readers get a story about first contact, pride, and the strain of judging an outsider by home rules.
2534-eugene-pickering:
Henry James sets this short tale at Homburg, a German spa town, in the days when its gaming rooms still drew fashionable crowds. The narrator meets Eugene Pickering, a young American of good fortune, and watches him fall under the spell of Madame Blumenthal, a brilliant older woman of the spa world.

Pickering sees in her a muse and a guide to a finer life, while the narrator doubts whether her charm hides a harder game. James writes with fine irony about youth, admiration, and the gap between what we dream of others and what they are. The story is a small, polished study of an American abroad learning to see clearly.
2572-on-the-decay-of-the-art-of-lying:
Mark Twain read this essay to the Historical and Antiquarian Club of Hartford, offering it for a thirty dollar prize that it did not take. Twain insists the custom of lying has not decayed at all: the lie, he says, is eternal as a virtue, a solace, and a refuge in need.

What has decayed, he argues with mock gravity, is the art of lying well, with grace and skill. Twain's jokes land on politicians, prudes, and polite society, all while he pretends to defend his subject. The essay is short, sly, and very funny, and it shows Twain turning a club talk into a small masterpiece of mischief.
2590-guy-mannering:
Walter Scott sets this novel on the wild Scottish coast, where the astrologer Guy Mannering casts a child's horoscope and foretells danger at three ages. The child, Harry Bertram, heir to Ellangowan, is stolen away, and his family falls to ruin under smugglers and schemers.

Years later the grown Harry returns, unknowing, among gypsies, soldiers, and the fierce Meg Merrilies, who guards his secret. Scott mixes romance, law, and low comedy with a love of border country. The book stands as one of his liveliest tales of lost heirs, second sight, and home regained.
2602-queen-sheba-s-ring:
H. Rider Haggard wrote this adventure around a ring that comes to a modern Englishman, launching a journey to a hidden African kingdom. The contents promise a sergeant's advice, a professor out shooting, a death wind, and an escape from Harmac, with lions' dens and oaths along the way.

Haggard's heroes face a queen's shadow, a rescue that fails, and a fate that dogs their steps. The tale mixes lost world romance with imperial adventure, in the author's brisk, earnest style. Readers who love King Solomon's Mines will find the same thrills here, with a ring at the heart of the mystery.
2714-long-live-the-king:
Mary Roberts Rinehart wrote this romance of a crown prince who runs away and sees the world, only to return disgraced and face terror at court. Chapters at a riding school, tea in a schoolroom, and a chancellor's visit mix boyish adventure with palace intrigue.

A letter, a fine night, and the right to live and love test the prince, while Nikky does a reckless thing and two prisoners wait in the park. Rinehart writes with warmth and suspense, in the Ruritanian manner. The book delights as a story of youth, duty, and a throne too heavy for a boy.
2885-the-house-of-the-wolfings-a-tale-of:
William Morris wrote The House of the Wolfings in prose and verse as a tale of the Wolfing house and all the kindreds of the Mark. The opening verses compare the world of men to a traveler passing a homestead left years before, its candles bright in a room beside the door that can never be entered again. The Mark's tribes face a Roman threat from the Mirkwood.

The story moves toward battle at the Slaughter Tofts, where tidings will tell whether the curse of the world has awakened and the serpent crawls in the thicket. Wood-wolves, shield people, spear kin, and horse kin march together. Morris's archaic style gives the tale its strange music, and it stands as a founding work of modern fantasy.
3093-the-eve-of-the-revolution-a-chronic:
Carl Becker wrote The Eve of the Revolution, volume eleven of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1918. Becker states his aim plainly, to convey not a record of what men did but a sense of how they thought and felt about what they did. The book recreates the intellectual atmosphere of the colonies on the breach with England.

Scenes include Boston courts adjourned for a fortnight at a time through Hutchinson and Oliver, to young John Adams's rising wrath. Adams fears the courts' inactivity will make a large chasm in his affairs, if not reduce him to distress, even as probate courts go on as if no Stamp Act existed. Becker's brief sketch remains a classic of intellectual history.
3101-washington-irving:
Warner wrote this life of Washington Irving for the American Men of Letters series. It came out in December 1881 as the first volume of that series. The book grew from a sketch written for the Geoffrey Crayon edition of Irving's works. That set ran to twenty-seven volumes, issued month by month from April 1880. The study later appeared again in a volume called Studies of Irving.

Warner follows Irving from his early New York sketches to his standing as America's first widely read man of letters. He weighs the life and the writing together. Readers who know Rip Van Winkle and the Sketch Book learn how a genial New York storyteller became a national figure.
3106-as-we-were-saying:
Charles Dudley Warner collected As We Were Saying with other essays in the backlog edition of his complete writings, published in 1904. Contents include Rose and Chrysanthemum, The Red Bonnet, and The Loss in Civilization. Social Screaming, Does Refinement Kill Individuality, The Directoire Gown, The Mystery of the Sex, The Clothes of Fiction, A Chewing Gum, Women in Congress, and Shall Women Propose follow. The essays began as magazine talk. A chewing-gum passage argues the habit is neither narcotic nor stimulant, soothing nor exciting, and differs totally from tobacco chewing or dipping, despite a popular impression that apothecaries sell it as medicine.

Warner's light essays treat manners, dress, and public life with humor. The volume shows the essayist behind the novelist, urbane and amused.
3133-baddeck-and-that-sort-of-thing:
Warner sketches a summer trip to Baddeck on Cape Breton Island in these light pieces. A preface addressed to Joseph H Twichell admits the debt plainly. Twichell taught him to say the name and showed him its place on the map. He also passed on a home missionary's tempting letter about trout and salmon. The usual demand for such sketches gathered them into this little volume.

The humor lies in modest travel: bad roads, plain lodgings, and grand scenery met without grandeur. Warner writes as a tourist who knows his own limits and enjoys them. The country wins in the end, quietly, while the traveler supplies the jokes.
364-the-mad-king:
Edgar Rice Burroughs sets this adventure in the small Balkan realm of Lutha, where a mad king has fled his guards. An American named Barney Custer, who looks just like King Leopold, is swept into court plots, escapes, and battles. Part one ends with a coronation; part two brings Barney back to face a firing squad and a traitor king.

Burroughs piles on sword fights, races to the capital, and last-minute rescues, all at a gallop. Barney's nerve and honor carry him where rank alone fails. The tale charms as pure swashbuckling fun, with a hero who must play king to save a land he barely knows.
388-the-crossing:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, follows a Kentucky youth from the Blue Ridge to Louisiana in this frontier epic. Born under King George III, the hero crosses the mountains, joins the fight for Kaskaskia, and drifts through Danville, St. Louis, and New Orleans. War, trade, and love mark his long road west.

Churchill writes in three books: borderland war, river drift, and Louisiana life. The hero meets soldiers, French settlers, and proud ladies, each testing his mettle. The novel stands as a broad tale of how the West was won, told with sweep and a fond eye for early American grit.
4050-mates-at-billabong:
A Billabong story for young readers follows Norah and her mates through station life in Australia. Chapters carry them from Norah's home and a first bath to cutting out cattle, a thunderstorm, the Billabong dance, and Christmas.

A letter home tells of arriving at Cunjee to find no one to meet her, then catching a lift in a dirty, springless buggy out to Billabong. The book mixes bush work, school holidays, and friendship with humor and warmth. Children who like horse and station tales will enjoy this cheerful entry in the Billabong series.
407-the-reporter-who-made-himself-king:
Richard Harding Davis tells of a young reporter who lands in a small island kingdom and, by nerve and press craft, makes himself its ruler. Davis opens with a jest on how reporters are trained, then lets his hero prove that bold news sense beats long training. The tale moves from newsroom talk to palace plots in brisk steps.

The reporter charms chiefs, fools rivals, and turns a coup into copy, all with a newspaperman's eye for a story. Davis writes with humor and dash, poking fun at both kings and papers. The short tale endures as a witty fantasy of the press age, when a bold man might still invent his own crown.
4312-a-life-s-morning:
George Gissing wrote this novel around Wilfrid Athel, an undergraduate sent down invalided soon after the start of Trinity term. The contents follow Beatrice Redwing, a conflict of opinions, the shadow of home, a visitor by express, and a sterner wooing. Later chapters bring Emily's decision, a cutting of the knot, renunciation, and a family conclave.

The title points to a morning of life, when choices still seem open and their costs are only dimly seen. Gissing traces Wilfrid and Emily through courtship, family pressure, and separation. The novel rewards readers who like Victorian stories of love weighed against duty, money, and pride.
4342-organic-gardener-s-composting:
Steve Solomon wrote this practical guide to composting for organic gardeners. He opens by asking what really happens when things rot, and he promises clear meanings for words like humus, compost, and organic matter. Garden books, he says, often confuse readers with vague terms such as stabilized humus.

Solomon explains the compost pile as a fast track for turning crude organic matter into something like soil. He treats the pile as a living process, not a nasty chore, and he gives plain directions for building and keeping it. The book suits gardeners who want rich soil without chemicals, and who want to understand why compost works.
4607-love-me-little-love-me-long:
Charles Reade tells this mild tale through Lucy Fountain, a young lady of beauty and standing who loses her mother, her sole surviving parent, nearly a quarter century before the main action. Her two trustees, Edward Fountain of Font Abbey and Mr. Bazalgette, a merchant married to her mother's half-sister, agree to share the burden. Lucy spends half the year with each trustee, until marriage takes her off their hands.

The story begins in Bazalgette's house, two years into that arrangement, and Reade lets chit-chat do the work of character. Men and women, he notes, do not come ticketed or with explanations in hand, so readers must judge them by talk. Readers get a gentle Victorian courtship novel, with guardians, suitors, and household talk, and with Reade's usual care for social detail and fair play.
4619-words-of-cheer-for-the-tempted-the-:
T. S. Arthur edited Words of Cheer for the Tempted, the Toiling, and the Sorrowing, published at Philadelphia in 1856. Every life, he says, alternates easy, blossom-strewn ways with hard, rough going, and bright days with storm-blackened ones to follow. On rough roads under a darkened sky, courage falters and trembles, and trusting eyes fail to glimpse the sun shining past the cloud veil.

Yet Arthur insists the rugged path winds steadily upward, and the broad sky still glitters in light. Readers are urged to keep faith in the God who feeds young lions, clothes fields, binds broken hearts, and gives joy to mourners. The volume gathers short pieces meant to be read in trouble, one by one. It suits readers of Victorian devotional writing, and anyone who wants plain, hopeful counsel for hard days.
4632-the-good-time-coming:
T. S. Arthur published The Good Time Coming at Boston and Philadelphia in 1855. His preface says life is a mystery to all, and the deeper a striving spirit sinks into selfish instincts, the more profound the mystery grows. How earnestly we fix our eyes on the slowly advancing future, impatiently waiting for that good time coming which never comes, while years glide by, beginning in hope and ending in disappointment.

Strange, Arthur says, that we gain so little true wisdom amid sharp disappointments at almost every turn. He too has long been an anxious waiter for the good time coming, which has not yet arrived. Yet hope should not die because of disappointment. There is a good time coming for each of us, if we work and wait patiently, and look in the right direction. Readers get an earnest Victorian moral book about hope, work, and patience.
504-the-fifth-string:
John Philip Sousa, famed for marches, writes this short novel of a violinist and a devil's bargain. Diotti, a star player fresh from Europe's courts, comes to America under impresario Henry Perkins. At a New York reception he charms society, but a fifth string on his violin holds a strange power over love and fate.

Sousa mixes concert scenes, social satire, and a touch of the supernatural. Diotti must learn that art bought at a price costs more than fame. The book charms as a light, musical fantasy by a man who knew the concert world from the podium.
5083-the-man-of-feeling:
Henry Mackenzie's short novel, first published in 1771, follows Harley, a young man of tender feeling who travels from the country to London and back. The story survives as a set of fragments, each episode showing Harley moved by the sorrows of strangers: a beggar, a fallen woman, a mad girl, and soldiers returned from war.

Mackenzie made feeling itself the hero, and the book became a landmark of the sentimental novel. Modern readers will find its earnest emotion old-fashioned at times. Its short scenes still show how eighteenth-century writers asked readers to judge character by compassion rather than by wit or wealth.
5116-pragmatism-a-new-name-for-some-old-:
William James delivered these lectures at the Lowell Institute in Boston in late 1906 and at Columbia University in early 1907. In them he presents pragmatism as a way of settling disputes about ideas: judge a belief by the practical difference it makes in life, rather than by abstract argument alone.

James applies that test to questions of truth, belief, religion, and human nature, arguing with philosophers he admired and those he opposed. The lectures read as spoken talks, direct and full of examples, and they remain a clear entry point into a philosophy that measures ideas by their consequences.
5124-henrietta-s-wish-or-domineering:
Charlotte M. Yonge's domestic novel follows Henrietta and the family circle around her, beginning with a summer arrival at Teignmouth on the Devon coast. Its second title, Domineering, points to the book's central tension: strong wills within a household. The harm appears when one person's wishes override the rest.

Yonge traces courtship, friendship, and family duty through small, telling scenes of everyday life. The novel belongs to her long series of moral family stories. It will appeal to readers who enjoy nineteenth-century domestic fiction where character is tested at home rather than on a battlefield.
5180-children-s-internet-protection-act-:
This court opinion, issued on May 31, 2002, by a three-judge court in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, decides challenges to the Children's Internet Protection Act. The American Library Association, Multnomah County Public Library, and others sued the United States, arguing that the law's conditions on library funding violated the First Amendment.

Judges Becker, Fullam, and Bartle set out the statutory framework, findings of fact, and their reasoning on filtering in public libraries. The opinion is a primary legal document, useful for readers studying internet freedom, library policy, and how courts weighed free speech against the protection of children online.
5351-if-i-were-king:
Justin Huntly McCarthy's If I Were King, published in 1901. It is dedicated to the loveliest lady this side of heaven, and opens with its famous refrain: if I were king, what tributary nations would I bring to stoop before your sceptre? Beneath your feet the poet would fling treasures, stars as pearls upon a string, and the world as a ruby for a finger ring.

McCarthy, a playwright and novelist, turns the romantic boast into a historical romance of Francois Villon and the Paris of Louis XI. Readers get a swashbuckling tale of a poet made king for a day, in which love, wit, and danger carry the story to its gallant end.
5500-the-advancement-of-learning:
Francis Bacon wrote The Advancement of Learning as a survey of human knowledge, addressed to the king in two books covering divine and human learning. This edition, transcribed from the 1893 Cassell publication, presents Bacon's argument that learning had been neglected and misused, and that a true account of its branches would serve both church and state.

Bacon maps the fields of knowledge, praises their uses, and criticizes empty disputes that produce heat without light. Readers get a founding text of modern thought about science and education, written in rich early modern prose. It remains a landmark for anyone tracing how knowledge came to be organized.
5774-they-call-me-carpenter-a-tale-of-th:
Upton Sinclair imagines a second coming in modern America in They Call Me Carpenter, published in New York in 1922. The narrator's strange adventure begins with a motion picture made in Germany, seen three years after the end of the First World War. From that screen, a carpenter figure steps into contemporary life, and Sinclair uses him to judge wealth, churches, studios, and politics.

The volume offers a provocative fable, earnest and satirical by turns, in which ancient teachings meet modern headlines. Sinclair writes plainly, letting the carpenter's simple questions expose greed and hypocrisy. The novel suits readers of social satire and religious fiction, and it remains a bold example of a novelist using fantasy to preach reform.
608-areopagitica-a-speech-for-the-libert:
John Milton pleads for free printing in this 1644 speech to Parliament, unlicensed itself by design. Milton argues that complaints freely heard, deeply weighed, and swiftly reformed mark the utmost bound of civil liberty. He warns that licensing books before print strangles truth more than any heresy.

Milton writes in grand, rolling prose, full of classical allusion and moral fire. His image of truth as a wounded body, scattered yet living, ranks among English prose's finest. The tract endures as a founding text of free speech, where a poet defends the press against its own Parliament.
610-idylls-of-the-king:
Alfred, Lord Tennyson retells Arthur's rise and fall in twelve linked poems in this Victorian epic. The Coming of Arthur opens the cycle; Gareth, Geraint, Balin, Merlin, Lancelot, and the Holy Grail follow; Guinevere and The Passing of Arthur close it. A dedication mourns Prince Albert as an ideal knight.

Tennyson writes in rich, musical blank verse, keen on honor, love, and betrayal. Camelot's glory fades as vows break and trust dies. The poems endures as the great Victorian Arthurian work, where a king's dream of order meets human frailty.
6118-the-rose-in-the-ring:
George Barr McCutcheon sets The Rose in the Ring amid circus folk, opening with a fugitive, a dressing tent, and David entering the sawdust ring. A stranger appears, something is learned about the Braddocks, and David Jenison's story unfolds beside the brothers Cronk.

An invitation to supper, a thief in the night, love winging a timid dart, and artful Dick going visiting lead to a sale. The second book gives the daughter of Colonel Grand, a stranger at the hall, a man who served his time, and a telegram delivered. McCutcheon mixes circus color with romance and debt.
6382-bat-wing:
Sax Rohmer opens toward six on a hot summer evening, with Paul Harley of Chancery Lane seated in his private office reading. Harley, detective hero of the tale, is summoned to Cray's Folly. There a shadow on a blind, cast by a woman raising her arms in a peculiar fashion, looks remarkably like a bat. The contents promise a voodoo swamp, a vampire bat, Val Beverley, a barrier, the Lavender Arms, and the call of M'Kombo.

Obeah, a night walker, morning mists, Ysola Camber, unrest, and a night of full moon follow, with Inspector Aylesbury of Market Hilton, a Spanish cigarette, and the wing of a bat. Colin Camber's secret, a Lee Enfield rifle, and a seventh yew tree lead to confession and experiment. Rohmer writes a thriller of West Indian magic and English country houses, where fear of Camber puzzles even Harley's specialised mind.
6476-himalayan-journals-volume-1-or-note:
Joseph Dalton Hooker's Himalayan Journals, volume one, first published in 1854 and dedicated to Charles Darwin, opens in the Sunderbunds and Calcutta Botanic Garden. Hooker, fresh from Antarctic voyaging with Sir James Ross, where botany was his chief pursuit, desired to add to his knowledge of natural history in India. The volume's first chapter runs through Burdwan, a rajah's gardens and menagerie, coal beds, lac insects, camels, and effloresced soda on soil.

Mahowa oil, Jains, and the ascent of Paras nath follow, with Doomree table land, hot springs, wild peacock, poppy fields, and the geography of Behar and Central India. A mid passage climbs to Kursiong bungalow, superbly placed on a narrow ridge, west window over the Balasun valley, east over the Mahanuddee. Hooker writes a naturalist's journal, plant by plant, valley by valley.
6477-himalayan-journals-volume-2-or-note:
Joseph Dalton Hooker's Himalayan Journals, volume two, first published in 1854, opens at chapter eighteen with arrangements for a second journey into Sikkim. Opposition of the Dewan, Lassoo Kajee, Tendong, a legend of flood, the Lama of Silok foke, Namtchi, and the Tchebu Lama fill the early pages. A gigantic oak, Teesta valley, commencement of rains, and ascent to Lathiang follow. Bad roads, orchids, and opposition of lamas slow the party.

Lepchas swim the Teesta, moxa treats sprains, and Singtam offers a grand view of Kinchinjunga, with wild men, landslips, bees' nests, and honey seekers. Choongtam brings rhododendrons, yew, venomous snakes, and hornets, with a temple and Tibetan salute. A mid passage tabulates thermometer readings and elevations across July and October, mean temperature falling from fifty to forty one degrees. Hooker writes high Himalaya as measurement and wonder.
6478-himalayan-journals-complete-or-note:
J. D. Hooker's complete Himalayan Journals, in the 1891 edition, gathers his notes as a naturalist in Bengal, the Sikkim and Nepal Himalayas, and the Khasia mountains. The opening chapters run as before. Sunderbunds vegetation, Calcutta Botanic Garden, Burdwan, a rajah's gardens and menagerie, coal beds, lac insects, camels, and effloresced soda on soil come first. Then come Mahowa oil, Jains, and the ascent of Paras nath. Doomree, hot springs, wild peacock, and poppy fields follow.

A mid passage measures air at a high pass, comparing vapour and humidity with Calcutta at the same hour. It then waits for coolies among rocks identical in natural history and geology to Kambachen pass. Hooker bids adieu to the sublime and majestic peak of Junnoo and continues four miles at nearly the same level. The complete edition lets a reader follow the whole journey, plant, rock, and weather together.
6522-fruit-gathering:
Rabindranath Tagore, writing in his own English from Bengali, offers short poems that treat a life like fruit ripening on a branch. Early verses speak of youth as a flower that drops a petal or two without loss, while later ones speak of age as fruit that holds nothing back. The garden, the river, and the evening wind run through the whole set.

Each poem is brief, yet it carries a full turn of feeling, from longing and loss to quiet surrender and joy. Tagore keeps the images plain and close to hand, so the sense lands at once rather than through hard thought. Fruit-Gathering reads as a small book of songs for the late season of a life.
655-life-and-letters-of-robert-browning:
Mrs. Sutherland Orr writes Robert Browning's life and letters in this second edition, prefaced in April 1891. Letters given by their recipients or copied by Browning's sister fill the volume, tracing the poet from family origins and boyhood through marriage and fame. Miss Browning's memory, Orr notes, was the only record of his youth.

Orr writes with careful, devoted prose, letting Browning's own words carry much of the tale. Chapters follow his grandfather, his father, and his early verse. The book serves as a key early biography, where a friend's care preserves a poet's voice for later readers.
656-life-of-robert-browning:
William Sharp writes a concise life of Robert Browning, the poet of dramatic monologues, from his London youth to his marriage with Elizabeth Barrett and his long Italian years. Sharp keeps the story clear and brief. Sharp, a Scottish critic, wrote short lives of poets for a wide audience.

Browning's poems, from early experiments to the great monologues, are set beside the life that shaped them. The book suits readers who want a first biography of Browning without the bulk of a full scholarly life. Browning's marriage to Elizabeth Barrett, and their life in Florence, gives the life its romance.
6689-fielding:
Austin Dobson writes the life of Henry Fielding for the English Men of Letters series, with a focus on fact over criticism. He notes that Fielding's works have already been well judged by many writers. Leslie Stephen is latest among them. So Dobson turns to biography instead. He checks tales about Fielding, corrects slips in older lives, and adds new details.

The memoir that follows traces Fielding from youth to novelist and magistrate, with care for dates and sources. Dobson's tone is modest, learned, and clear. Fielding is a solid, readable life of the Tom Jones author, useful to any reader who wants the man behind the novels.
6737-the-social-cancer-a-complete-englis:
Charles Derbyshire gives a complete English version of José Rizal's Noli Me Tangere, called here The Social Cancer, issued in Manila and New York in 1912. A companion volume, The Reign of Greed, renders the sequel, El Filibusterismo. The translator's introduction opens with a train image: readers fly through centuries in minutes, while those who live them feel each day drag.

Rizal's novel shows Philippine life under Spanish rule, with priests, officials, lovers, and rebels caught in a rotting social order. Its power helped stir a nation toward freedom. The Social Cancer is a landmark novel of colonial protest, still fierce and moving today.
6912-school-and-home-cooking:
Carlotta Greer, head of foods and household management at East Technical High School in Cleveland, wrote this text for pupils to use both at school and at home. Its use ends note taking, which Greer calls dictation in disguise, and so saves much time. Lessons follow a psychological method, starting from what lies within a beginner's own life and building outward to new needs.

Foods rich in each foodstuff are grouped in a logical order, while each lesson approaches its dish in the order a learner can grasp. The book gives enough dishes and hand processes to train a pupil well, and an illustration shows a corner of Washington's kitchen at Mount Vernon. It is a plain, practical school book for the kitchen.
7047-back-to-billabong:
Mary Grant Bruce brings her folk back to Billabong in 1921, opening with a Mackellar verse on a brown land of open spaces, gaunt forest, and treeless plain. If once loved, the verse says, that land must draw its lovers back again. Contents run from Lancaster Gate in London through the Rainhams, playing truant, coming home, and the turn of fortune's wheel, to sailing orders and watch dogs.

Tommy boards a strange taxi, Australia welcomes the travelers, and Billabong itself appears, with colonial experiences, influenza and furniture, and the home on the creek. The Cunjee races, Wally's race ride, and building up again close the tale. A schoolroom row over a map opens the book, with red haired, snub nosed Wilfred defiant at his table.
7058-mankind-in-the-making:
H G Wells presents Mankind in the Making as a companion to Anticipations and the pamphlet The Discovery of the Future. Read alongside those earlier works, it sets out a broad account of how societies grow and how people should act within public life. Wells takes up questions of society and government from a fresh vantage, treating the entire social and political order as parts of a single unfolding pattern.

All social and political activities, he argues, stand in a defined relation to that scheme, and to this method and trend he directs the reader's attention. The preface asks to save misunderstanding by stating aim and scope at the outset. The book is Wells the prophet at work, planning how a species might consciously shape its own future.
7354-on-something:
H. Belloc's On Something, dedicated to somebody, gathers essays on a plea for the simpler drama, a notebook, and unknown people. A Van Tromp, threepenny bits, the hotel at Palma and a proposed guide-book, and the death of wandering Peter follow. The tree of knowledge, a Norfolk man, the odd people, and a letter of advice and apology to a young burglar follow. The monkey question, the empire builder, Caedwalla, a unit of England, the relic, and the ironmonger complete the set.

A force in Gaul, bridges, a blue book, Perigueux of the Perigord, the position, home, the way to fairyland, and a portrait of a child close a book that wanders by design. Belloc writes on whatever catches his eye, with wit, learning, and strong opinion. The essays reward readers who enjoy a companionable, combative mind.
741-thomas-hart-benton-s-remarks-to-the-:
Thomas Hart Benton rose in the Senate on 12 January 1837 to move that a censure of President Jackson be expunged from the journal. Three years earlier, he notes, the Senate had passed the resolve, and at once he gave notice that he would seek its erasure. He argues that the resolve was unjust, and that time has proven his case.

Benton's speech is a long, dogged defence of Jackson and of the Senate's right to correct its own record. He speaks with the bluntness of a western senator sure of his ground. The text is a key document of the Bank War era, showing how party feeling, pride, and procedure shaped one of the fiercest fights of the age.
8114-personal-recollections-abridged-chi:
Charlotte Elizabeth, the evangelical writer, wrote Personal Recollections, here abridged chiefly in parts pertaining to political and other controversies prevalent in Great Britain at the time. Her letters trace childhood, youth, and early days: martyrs' prison and palace gardens, music and study, politics and Protestantism. Private journals and romance, loss of hearing, rural life, and ruinous customs such as tight-lacing. The abridgement keeps the controversial heart of the book.

Charlotte Elizabeth writes as a convert and campaigner, frank about her convictions and her quarrels. Her recollections give a vivid view of evangelical and political life in early Victorian Britain. For readers of women's autobiography and religious history, the volume offers a strong, opinionated, and very personal witness.
8131-the-misses-mallett-the-bridge-divid:
E. H. Young divided this novel into three books: Rose, Henrietta, and Rose and Henrietta, following two sisters whose lives a bridge divides. The opening paints a spring day on high land above a distant channel, with gorse, larch tassels, celandines, sheep and lambs, and hills veiled in blue. From that landscape, the story turns to the sisters' choices, marriages, and the distance that grows between them.

Young writes with lyrical attention to place and to women's inner lives, in the tradition of the English domestic novel. The bridge of the title stands for the separations, of temperament, marriage, and fate, that part even close sisters. For readers of early twentieth-century women's fiction, it is a beautifully observed and quietly moving book.
8147-the-man-who-would-be-king:
Rudyard Kipling's tale follows two British adventurers, Daniel Dravot and Peachey Carnehan, who set out to make themselves kings in Kafiristan, a remote land beyond Afghanistan. The narrator, a journalist, first meets them as vagabonds with a grand scheme, and later hears the end of it from a broken, half-mad survivor. The epigraph quotes the Law of their brotherhood: brother to a prince and fellow to a beggar, if he be found worthy.

Dravot does become a king, with army, law-courts, revenue, and policy complete, until pride and a forbidden marriage undo him. Kipling's story is a parable of empire and ambition, told with grim humour. It remains one of his most famous works, and a warning about the dream of ruling others.
8162-modern-painting:
George Moore wrote Modern Painting from chapters first published in The Speaker, gathered in the sequence originally intended. And dedicated the book to Sir William Eden, saying its subject had been the subject of nearly all their conversations. His contents cover Whistler, Chavannes, Millet, and Manet, the failure of the nineteenth century, and artistic education, among other topics. Moore writes as a novelist turned critic, with strong likes and dislikes.

The book argues for modern French painting against academic convention, in prose that is itself a performance. Moore's judgments can be fierce, but they are never dull. For readers of art criticism, it remains a vivid document of the moment when Impressionism and its successors were still fighting for acceptance.
8444-c-sar-or-nothing:
Pío Baroja's novel Cæsar or Nothing, translated from Spanish by Louis How, opens with a prologue and a first part set in Rome. Contents follow the Paris-Ventimiglia express, an extraordinary family, and Cæsar Moncada. They move on to people who pass close by, the Abbé Preciozi, and the little interests of people in a Roman hotel, before old palaces, old salons, and old ladies.

Baroja, a leading Spanish novelist of the Generation of 1898, writes of ambition and will, with a hero who would be Caesar or nothing.
